READING

**The financial gap**

TARNSIDE costs £1,730,000. VELLACOTT costs £2,680,000 net after the Brindlemere sale, a difference of £950,000. The fuel saving of £190,000 a year means VELLACOTT recoups that extra spend in exactly five years at current prices. Fuel prices may move either way; the arithmetic at today's prices is a break-even around 2032. That is not a short horizon for an operator running one vessel on a year-round statutory route, but it is a real one.

The £190,000 figure also compounds in VELLACOTT's favour indefinitely thereafter. The Suilvenaig hull is nine years old against the Brindlemere's thirty-one. Even with new engines, the Brindlemere will face growing maintenance costs and diminishing residual value over the next decade. In a twenty-year view VELLACOTT is clearly superior financially. The question is whether the near-term risks can be managed.

**The insurance gap**

A broker who has not yet quoted on the Suilvenaig is a material unknown. Marine insurance for a different vessel class, particularly one whose operation requires a specialist endorsement currently held by none of your masters, may come in materially above current terms—or may carry conditions that affect trading. Committing £3,050,000 to purchase, and a further £240,000 to permanent infrastructure at Ardvraich, before that quote exists is building a financial case on a number that does not yet exist. If the insurance premium neutralises even half the annual fuel saving, the five-year payback extends to ten, and the case for VELLACOTT weakens sharply.

**The master problem**

This is the more acute operational concern. You have nine masters now. Two will retire rather than take the endorsement course. That leaves seven, every one of whom must complete a six-week course before they can lawfully take the wheel of the Suilvenaig. In the period between handover (November 2026) and the opening of the busy season (May 2027) you have roughly twenty-four weeks. At six weeks per person, and assuming you can run two masters through the course simultaneously without compromising cover, you could qualify four masters before summer 2027 opens. That is the absolute minimum to hold an eleven-crossing-per-day summer schedule with any margin for sickness or leave. The remaining three would trail through during winter 2027–28.

More pressingly: before anyone can operate the Suilvenaig at all, at least one master must hold the endorsement. That means dispatching someone on the course immediately on or after handover, qualifying them around early January 2027, and then running the vessel on a single qualified master while the others train in rotation. For a single-vessel, year-round-licence operation with seven people ashore and no spare hull, that is a precarious position to hold for the better part of two years.

TARNSIDE leaves all nine masters in place, keeps the rota intact, and involves no change to crew qualifications.

**The yard period**

Twelve weeks from 5 January 2027 runs to approximately 30 March 2027. That is entirely within the low-season timetable of five crossings a day, and the charter from Sorrelbank Marine at £310,000 is already agreed in principle. The operational disruption of TARNSIDE is real but bounded and covered.

**The Ardvraich linkspan**

£240,000 of infrastructure work has its own timeline and planning risk. The quotation covers cost but says nothing about programme. If the linkspan work slips, the Suilvenaig cannot operate on arrival. That is another dependency TARNSIDE does not carry.

**The Kittiwake valuation**

The £610,000 valuation holds until 11 February 2027. If VELLACOTT is chosen and the Brindlemere sale is delayed—by, for instance, the distraction of running a new vessel on a thin qualified-master rota—the window for achieving that valuation closes. A revised valuation could be lower, widening the net cost of VELLACOTT further. This is a minor dependency but worth noting.

**Summary**

VELLACOTT is the better vessel and, over a long enough horizon, the better investment. The fuel saving is real, the hull age advantage is real, and the absence of a yard period in 2027 is genuinely attractive. In a world where the insurance quote had been received and was acceptable, and where the full nine masters were willing to train, I would look harder at it.

But the insurance figure does not exist, and two masters will not train. The combination—unknown insurance terms on a £3,050,000 commitment, a master rota reduced to seven with every one of those seven needing a six-week endorsement before the vessel can be operated, and permanent infrastructure works at Ardvraich with no stated programme—represents an accumulation of unresolved dependencies that a single-vessel, year-round-licence operation cannot comfortably carry simultaneously.

TARNSIDE delivers a known outcome: confirmed cost, confirmed insurance, confirmed crew, low-season yard slot, agreed charter cover. The fuel penalty is real and the hull is ageing, but neither is an immediate crisis, and neither is unquantified.

---

READING
  VELLACOTT is the superior vessel and better long-term investment on fuel savings and hull age, but it rests on an insurance figure that does not yet exist and requires a master rota of nine to absorb two retirements and seven six-week endorsement courses without dropping below the minimum needed to hold an eleven-crossing summer schedule; TARNSIDE delivers a fully costed, fully crewed, insurance-confirmed outcome at £950,000 less, using a low-season yard slot already covered by a chartered relief vessel, making it the executable choice against an uncertain but genuinely attractive alternative.

CALL
  TARNSIDE

GROUNDS
  The unquoted insurance position on the Suilvenaig, taken together with the loss of two masters from nine and the requirement for every remaining master to complete a six-week endorsement course, leaves VELLACOTT resting on too many simultaneous unresolved dependencies for a single-vessel operation holding a year-round licence to accept responsibly.
